title: Connes Distance in Discrete-Time Quantum Walks
authors: Rayan Trabelsi, A. F. Reyes-Lega, Pablo Arrighi
abstract: We study the geometric spread of discrete-time quantum walks using Connes' distance formula. We introduce its discrete analogue by adapting the continuous spectral metric to the lattice, with the Dirac operator replaced by the unitary step operator. Focusing first on a (2+1)-dimensional quantum walk, we evaluate the dynamical spread of localized wavepackets to compare propagation in free space against that under a uniform magnetic field. We find that while the free walk shows linear ballistic growth, gauge-induced phases in the magnetic walk constrain the admissible test operators, suppressing the long-time geometric expansion. Furthermore, we apply this discrete framework to a (1+1)-dimensional plastic quantum walk simulating an inhomogeneous spatial metric. The results demonstrate that the discrete Connes distance naturally captures the underlying spatially varying metric, providing a robust measure of the wavepacket's spread that adapts directly to the local simulated geometry.
summary: This work develops a discrete analogue of Connes' distance to measure the geometric spread of quantum walks on lattices. By applying this metric to 2+1D and 1+1D models, the authors demonstrate that the distance quantifies how magnetic fields constrain propagation and how the metric naturally adapts to spatially varying geometries.
main_problem: The paper investigates the geometric spread of discrete-time quantum walks by adapting Connes' distance formula from continuous spectral geometry to a discrete lattice setting.
main_result: The discrete Connes distance successfully measures wavepacket spread, showing that magnetic fields suppress long-time expansion, and the framework naturally captures inhomogeneous spatial metrics.
method: The authors adapt the Connes distance, defined via spectral triples, by replacing the continuous Dirac operator with a discrete unitary step operator, analyzing the resulting commutator norms.
model_or_system: The study focuses on discrete-time quantum walks (DTQWs) simulating systems ranging from free particles in (2+1)D space to walks on lattices simulating inhomogeneous metrics in (1+1)D.
key_observables: Connes Distance ($d_D$), dynamical spread of Gaussian wavepackets, and the commutator norm of the step operator.
important_parameters: Dimensionality (1+1D, 2+1D), magnetic field strength (gauge-induced phases), and the time step $\epsilon$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the convergence of the discrete step operator to the continuous Dirac Hamiltonian in the limit $\epsilon 	o 0$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the discrete analogue of the Connes distance, then applying it to analyze the 2+1D case (free vs. magnetic field), and finally extending the framework to model inhomogeneous metrics in 1+1D using convex optimization.
why_interesting: The application of Noncommutative Geometry tools like Connes' distance to quantum walks provides a powerful, mathematically rigorous way to quantify geometric effects (like magnetic fields or varying metrics) on quantum transport.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Wavepacket probability densities for the discrete quantum walk. (a) Initial localized Gaussian state at t = 0. (b) Free walk evolution at N = 20 showing the macroscopic ballistic ring. (c) Magnetic walk evolution at N = 20 demonstrating spatial suppression and Landau-like confinement.

Figure 2. (a) Numerical evaluation of the Connes distance for the free and magnetic quantum walks compared to their theoretical limits. (b) The numerical-to-asymptotic ratio R(N) for the free walk, which rapidly stabilizes near 1.12.

Figure 3. Spread of the homogeneous 1+1D plastic quantum walk. (a) The numerical Connes distance plotted against walk steps N for different values of θ. (b) The spatial probability density PN(x) at N = 12 for different values of θ. The dotted vertical lines are the causal edges x = ±2Nϵ cos θ. (c) Connes distance as a function of the coin parameter θ at fixed N, comparing the numerical values (colored markers) with the analytical asymptotic prediction.

Figure 4. Numerical evaluation of the Connes distance in an inhomogeneous spatial metric. (a) Spatial profiles of the speed of light c(x) = cos θ(x) (setting κ = 1), which encode the simulated metric g11. (b) Distorted wavepacket probability densities PN(x) at N = 30. (c) The numerical Connes distance plotted against walk steps N.
